To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

TMEM258, a gene within a complex locus, regulates intestinal inflammation through a previously unappreciated mechanism of endoplasmic stress control and that the identification of TMEM258 as a key regulator of intestinal inflammation provides an opportunity to develop novel therapies for inflammatory bowel disease and other inflammatory diseases.
TMEM258 haploinsufficiency results in ER stress, intestinal inflammation, and colitis.
TMEM258 deficiency causes severe ER stress, intestinal inflammation, and colitis.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of the oligosacharyltransferase (OST) complex in the regulation of intestinal inflammation.
the molecular and cellular biology of the ER.
the identification of the genetic basis of complex diseases, with particular focus on the inflammatory bowel diseases (Crohn’s disease and ulcerative colitis).
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the TMEM258 gene encodes a component of the oligo-saccharide transferase complex that regulates intestinal inflammation.

TMEM258, a gene within a gene-dense region associated with inflammatory bowel diseases, rheumatoid diseases, and coronary artery diseases, is required for ER homeostasis in intestinal epithelial cells.
TMEM258 deficiency results in ER stress in intestinal cells, which leads to apoptosis.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

TMEM258 haploinsufficiency results in a loss-of-function phenotype that is characterized by severe intestinal inflammation, which is associated with unresolved ER stress and apoptosis in colonic epithelial cells.
TMEM258 deficiency leads to ER stress and intestinal inflammation.
TMEM258 haploinsufficiency is sufficient to cause severe intestinal inflammation, which is due to a defect in N-linked glycosylation.
The main takeaway from our work is that
TMEM258 deficiency results in severe intestinal inflammation in mice, and this is due to unresolved endoplasmatic reticulum (or ER) stress.
the genetic association of TMEM258 to inflammatory bowel disease is likely to reflect a direct role of TMEM258 in intestinal homeostasis, rather than a role in the inflammatory response.
TMEM258, which has not been previously linked to disease, is a central regulator of ER stress and intestinal homeostatic processes.
